HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH  Cr.R. No.3360/2019  (Rehmatali vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh)
 Indore
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
Smt. Nisha Tanwar, learned Panel Lawyer for the  respondent/State.
 ORDER

Applicant/accused has preferred this revision petition under Section 397 read with Section 401 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (for short "The Code") against the order dated 27/04/2019 passed by Special Judge (NDPS ACT), District Mandsaur, in Special Sessions Trial No.35/2019,
whereby the trial Court has rejected the application filed on behalf of the applicant/accused praying for re-testing of second sample of the seized contraband article from the Central Revenues and Control Laboratory (CRCL), New Delhi.

entities.text: Central Revenues and Control Laboratory (CRCL), New Delhi
entities.label: ORG

sentences.text: 02. Brief facts of the case are that on 13/10/2018, at about 3.40 pm, 4.00 kgs of smack has been seized from the possession of the applicant which was being transported in his Maruti Alto car bearing Registration No.MP 14 CC 2397.
Sample of the contraband article has been taken and sent for examination to Regional Forensic Laboratory, Rao, District Indore.
Wherein, on examination, it has been found to be Di-acetyl Morphine (smack).
After completion of investigation, charge-sheet has been filed on 09/04/2019 before the Special Court (NDPS), Mandsaur.
On 15/04/2019, the applicant/accused had moved an application for sending the second sample of seized contraband for analysis to CRCL, New Delhi.

03. Learned trial Judge, rejected the application on the context of law laid down by Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of 'Thana Singh vs. Central Bureau of Narcotics, reported as (2013)2 SCC 590 holding that under extremely exceptional circumstances the re-testing of second sample of the seized contraband article can be ordered and there is no such circumstance available in the present case.

entities.text: Thana Singh vs. Central Bureau of Narcotics, reported as (2013)2 SCC 590
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 04. I have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the impugned order.

sentences.text: It is not disputed that in the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (for short 'NDPS Act') itself there is no such provision of permitting re-testing of samples of seized contraband articles.

entities.text: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: In the case of Thana Singh Vs. CBN (Supra), the Hon'ble Apex Court issued the guidelines for re- testing /re-sampling of the contraband articles seized under the 'NDPS Act'.
Relevant paragraphs of the judgment is reproduced hereunder:-
" 24. The NDPS Act itself does not permit re-sampling or re-testing of samples.

Yet,
there has been a trend to the contrary; NDPS courts have been consistently obliging to applications for re-testing and re- sampling.
These applications add to delays as they are often received at advanced stages of trials after significant elapse of time.

NDPS courts seem to be permitting re-testing nonetheless by taking resort to either some High Court judgments [See: State of Kerala Vs. Deepak. P. Shah[5]; Nihal Khan Vs. The State (Govt. of NCT Delhi)[6]] or perhaps to Sections 79 and 80 of the NDPS Act which permit application of the Customs Act, 1962 and the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.

entities.text: State of Kerala Vs. Deepak. P. Shah[5]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Nihal Khan Vs. The State (Govt. of NCT Delhi)[6
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: While re-testing may be an important right of an accused, the haphazard manner in which the right is imported from other legislations without its accompanying restrictions, however, is impermissible.

Under the NDPS Act,
re-testing and re-sampling is rampant at every stage of the trial contrary to other legislations which define a specific time-frame within which the right may be available.
Besides, reverence must also be given to the wisdom of the Legislature when it expressly omits a provision, which otherwise appears as a standard one in other legislations.

The Legislature, unlike for the NDPS Act, enacted Section 25(4) of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and Rule 56 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944, permitting a time period of thirty, ten and twenty days respectively for filing an application for re- testing.
25. Hence, it is imperative to define re-testing rights, if at all, as an amalgamation of the above- stated factors.

Further, in light of Section 52A of the NDPS Act, which permits swift disposal of some hazardous substances, the time frame within which any application for re-testing may be permitted ought to be strictly defined.
xxx xxx xxx 27

. Therefore, keeping in mind the array of factors discussed above, we direct that,
after the completion of necessary tests by the concerned laboratories, results of the same must be furnished to all parties concerned with the matter.
Any requests as to re-testing/re-sampling shall not be entertained under the NDPS Act as a matter of course.

These may, however, be permitted, in extremely exceptional circumstances,
for cogent reasons to be recorded by the Presiding Judge.
An application in such rare cases must be made within a period of fifteen days of the receipt of the test report; no applications for re- testing/re-sampling shall be entertained thereafter.

However, in the absence of any compelling circumstances, any form of re-testing/re-sampling is strictly prohibited under the NDPS Act."

sentences.text: In the present case, learned counsel for the applicant has put forth his submissions that no contraband article has been recovered from the possession of the applicant.
The Police apprehended the applicant from Nahata Bhawan Square, Mandsaur and brought him to Police-Station and demanded illegal gratification of Rs.25.00 lakhs.
When he could not manage the payment of the aforesaid amount, then Police falsely implicated the applicant in the present crime alleging that 4.00 kgs of Smack has been recovered from his possession.

It is further submitted that according to the FSL report the seized contraband article contained 2.5% of Di-acetyl Morphine in it, whereas in normal course Smack Heroine contains 100% of Di-acetyl Morphine in it.

It is also submitted that from the photographs of seized article it appears that while weighing the contraband the colour of the contraband was pure white, whereas, the sample received by FSL in brown colour, therefore,
counsel

prayed that a second sample be taken out from the seized contraband and sent to CRCL,
New Delhi for another report.
07. Learned Panel Lawyer opposes the prayer by contending that no ground is available for sending the second sample to CRCL, New Delhi for re-testing hence he prays for rejection of the application.

08. After considering the arguments advanced by the learned counsel for the parties and looking to the facts and circumstances of the case, this Court is of the view that the grounds raised by the applicant are not sufficient to send the second sample to CRCL, New Delhi, for re-testing because there is no exceptional circumstance available for sending the second sample for re-testing.

Hence,
this Court is of the view that the trial Court has not committed any error in rejecting the application filed by the applicant.
08. Accordingly, Criminal Revision No.3360/2019 is hereby dismissed being devoid of merits.
Certified copy, as per Rules.
